beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: This indicator represents plant community responses to climate warming. It quantifies the positive deviation of the cumulative abundance of heat requirement plant indicator values in monitored vegetation compared to a reference community. Thus, this indicator is one-sided. 2. **Methods**: The data comes from field sampled plant community data from the Norwegian nature monitoring program ANO (Tingstad et al. 2019). We combine these community data with functional trait values on Heat requirement from Tyler et al. (2021). The indicator values are based on calculating cumulative abundance (see Framstad et al. 2022) of Heat requirement values for plant community data. Deviations in such an indicator beyond a certain range of indicator values indicate a directional shift in the plant community. As reference communities we use ‘generalized species lists’ underlying the Norwegian categorization system for eco-diversity (Halvorsen et al. 2020). 3. **Interpretation**: An indicator value of 1 indicates no discernible difference in the functional plant composition due to climate warming. Values decreasing toward zero reflect a shift in species composition and community trait values away from the reference state, as a response to warming. 4. **Results and development needs**: The indicator value for Norway as a whole is 0.41 [95%CI: 0.39-0.43], indicating that the functional plant community composition deviates more than accepted under good ecological condition. The result is driven by an increase in abundance of species in the plant community with high heat requirement values. To improve this indicator in the future, the perhaps most pressing issue it to regionalise the generalised species list, as currently they have a bias towards southern and eastern Norway. The indicator values also need validation against independent datasets.
indikatorenhet: Abundance data for vascular plants in ANO is given as % cover within a 1 m2 sample quadrat. This is transformed to relative abundance data per quadrat. Each ANO quadrat is classified to its respective ecosystem type according to ‘Nature in Norway’ (NiN; <https://artsdatabanken.no/NiN>). Environmental indicator values from Tyler et al. (2021) are given on an ordinal scale from 1 (lowest affinity to the respective variable) to n (highest affinity to the respective variable), the number of levels (n) varying between environmental indicators.
innsamlingsmetode: At every ANO site, the the plant community is recorded (presence and percent cover of every vascular plant species) in the central 1 sqm plot of each of systematically arranged 18 monitoring points.
dekket_tidsperiode: The ANO monitoring data available now represent one cycle of sampling from 2019-2024 comprising ca. 1000 sites across Norway. ANO has no defined end date. 2025 is the first year of repeated sampling for about 20% of the approximately 1000 ANO sites for all of mainland Norway (i.e. the Ecosystem Accounting Area). Annual sampling is spatially representative, in principle allowing to compute area-representative estimates for single years but also multiple-yr-reporting periods. The indicator at hand is calculated based on the ANO data from 2020-2024.
radata: The ANO data are openly available at https://kartkatalog.miljodirektoratet.no/Dataset/Details/2054. See @sec-about for detail on the other datasets.
arealrepresentativitet: The variable is scaled, transformed (piece-wise linear) and truncated at the initial ANO-point level and the indicator estimate is an arithmetic mean of all ANO-points.
referansetilstand: In Norway, the reference condition for natural ecosystems has been one of largely intact ecosystems without large-scale human modifications (Nybø and Evju 2017). The reference climate is from 1961-1990.
referanseverdier: Reference and limit values (scaling values) for functional plant community indicators are derived as the 0.025, 0.5, and 0.975 quantiles (lower limit values, reference value, upper limit value, respectively) from distributions of community weighted means of the respective plant indicators originating from bootstrapped generalized species lists. Bootstraps were set up with resampling of the original generalized species lists 1000 times. In every sample a random 1/3 of the original generalized species list was sampled (as ANO points on average contain roughly a third of the potential species richness in the generalized species lists -> local variation in species composition thus is large and needs to be reflected in the bootstraps), with the exception of dominant species (abundance value of 5 or higher in the original scale of the generalized species lists), which were retained in every sample. All reference distributions, and thus all scaling values are unique to NiN mapping units at a scale of 1:5000.
annen_informasjon: Uncertainties relate partly to sampling and observer variability (and possible observer bias) in the recording of the plant cover data. Presumably, there is also uncertainty related to the scoring of indicator values for species, and this will probably vary among species (cf. Tyler et al. 2021). These potential sources uncertainty can only be assumed and not quantified. Spatial variability as a source of uncertainty can be quantified. beskrivelse: Glaciers represents important structural elements in alpine ecosystems, providing melt water and local climate control. It is also a unique nature type and habitat in itself, with few, but very specialised, species living on or in association with the ice. Glaciers are permanently ice covered areas and they are sensitive to climate change, especially climate warming, which melts the ice. In Norway we have a rather detailed and precise map of the glacier cover or extent from the period 1947-1985. Here I use this data as a representation of the climatic reference condition (pre climate warming), and compare this with an updated glacier cover map from 2018-2019 to create a normalised ecosystem condition indicator. Glacier area and glacier area change is calculated for each unique combination of bioclimatic and geographical regions (referred to as _strata_). A threshold value (X~60~) have tentatively been defined as 60% remaining glacier area inside each EA with the interpretation that a 60% loss of glaciers inside each strata represents a scenario where the ecological functions provided by glaciers are clearly deteriorated. Indicator uncertainty originates from two sources. Firste we introduce a 3% error in the glacier cover estimates, based on the reported uncertainties in the mapping method. In practice we create a gaussian probability distribution (*n* = 1000, sd = 0.03 × mean), rather than a point estimate, to each strata. I then resample these probability distributions for each stratum n times, with n equal to the area weight, and combine these samples into a joint sample distribution for the next spatial aggregation level. This also introduces the second type of uncertainty, which is the spatial variation in indicator values across strata. The indicator is ready to be used. Future updates will require new maps of glacier cover in Norway, which is highly possible to produce from satellite imagery. I also include an analyses of the influence of using different areal weight, and different strata definitions. This work concludes that initial glacier extent should be used as area weights rather than total mountain area, and that the modifiable area unit problem is not having a very strong influence on the resulting aggregated probabilities. **Interpretation**: The indicator value represents the negative ecological effect of melting glacier ice, as a mean across the strata. It does NOT directly represent the area of remaining glacier ice. **Simplified workflow** 1. Import glacier cover maps from two time periods 2. Import delineations for bioclimatic regions and geographical regions and intersect to create strata 3. Import alpine ecosystem mask 4. Compile spatial dataset where each strata has data on strata category, glacier area at two time points and total mountain area. 5. Add 3% uncertainty to glacier cover estimates by replacing point estimate with a probability sample (n = 1000) 6. Normalise variable at strata level by scaling, transforming and truncating. 7. Make a weighted sample within strata and create a new, joint sampling distribution for a spatially aggregate indicator value for geographical regions. 8. Similarly, aggregate spatially from geographical region to national level. 9. Summarise national estimate and 50%CI in a table

beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: This indicator represents the proportion of the forest area with trees of all species with a diameter at breast height of at least 40 cm. In forests shaped by natural disturbances and succession, large trees are expected to occur to a much higher extent than today. Historical harvesting of large trees and short harvest rotations in current forestry tend to prevent trees from growing very large. 2. **Methods**: Data for this indicator come from the National Forest Inventory (NFI), where the diameter at breast height (dbh) of all trees larger than 5 cm dbh within the 250 m^2^ NFI plot has been recorded by current methods since the mid-1990s [@viken2021-feltinstruks]. 3. **Interpretation**: The share of forest with large trees will eventually be compared to a reference value for all forest, based on expert assessments supported by empirical data for near-natural forests and knowledge of ecosystem dynamics in intact forest ecosystems. Such reference values have not yet been determined for this indicator. 4. **Results and development needs**: Otherwise, the indicator is ready for use as a non-scaled variable. The indicator should not be used at a finer spatial resolution than allows for reliable estimates, probably regions.
indikatorenhet: The indicator is specified as the proportion (%) of NFI plots with at least one tree with dbh ≥ 40 cm.
dekket_tidsperiode: Data are available from the mid-1990s, when current recording methods were established. Annual estimates are possible due to representative sampling every year. For this indicator all data from each full inventory cycle of 5 years are used, starting in 2010. The data are representative for all forest land within the selected region. Spatial resolution should be limited to a resolution that allows reliable estimates, probably counties or ‘half-counties’.
radata: NA
referansetilstand: The reference condition is considered to be intact forest ecosystems, where effects of human activities are clearly subordinate to those of natural ecosystem processes and disturbances.
referanseverdier: An upper reference value (X100) has not yet been determined. It would probably be based on expert assessments supported by information on (1) the frequency of large trees in NFI plots assessed to be little affected by recent human activities, (2) the distribution of dominating tree species in various regions/counties, and (3) general assessments of natural forest dynamics and the effects on the size of trees. Reference values would be expert assessments without estimated uncertainty. The lower reference value (X0) is set to 0. For lack of better knowledge, the relationship between indicator values and ecosystem condition is assumed to be linear for values between X100 and X0. Hence, indicator values are scaled between 0 and 1 based on a linear scaling function between X0 and X100; scaled indicator values above 1 are truncated to 1.
annen_informasjon: Uncertainties relate to the variability in the frequency of large trees among NFI plots and measurement errors for trees within NFI plots. This combined uncertainty is quantified by bootstrapping. There will also be uncertainty related to the setting of the upper reference value and to the shape of the relationship between indicator values and ecosystem condition. These uncertainties will not be quantified.
pavirkningsfaktorer: Frequent natural disturbances, such as rock slides, fires, floods, or windthrows, will reduce the frequency of large trees (although large pines will often survive fires). Historical forestry practices of harvesting the largest trees or current clear-cutting with frequent recurrent harvesting will prevent the development of large trees. Human-induced climate change may result in more rapid tree growth with faster attainment of the dbh criterion for large trees. However, such climate change may also induce more frequent disturbances, drought events, or increased pressure of pathogens, all generally reducing the life span of forest trees.

beskrivelse: <!--# With a maximum of 300 words, describe the indicator in general terms as you would to a non-expert. Think of this as a kind of common language summary. Follow the four numbers sub-headers below. under point 2, it is possible under include a bullet point list of the specific steps in the workflow. --> 1. **Background and rationale**: The Eurasian lynx (*Lynx lynx*) is the largest feline species in the European landscape and the only native wild cat in Norway. As a "small big cat," it occupies a unique trophic niche, primarily hunting small ungulates such as roe deer through a characteristic stalking and ambush tactic [@breitenmoser2026_lynx]. In Norway, it lives mainly in forest areas over large parts of the country, and the densest populations are in Mid-Norway and eastern Norway. Lynx population dynamics are often influenced by the availability of staple prey and anthropogenic pressures, including habitat fragmentation and human-induced mortality. The indicator is part of the Norwegian Nature Index and is described on [Naturindeksen](https://naturindeks.no/Indicators/gaupe). 2. **Methods**: Indicator values for lynx abundance are taken from the Naturindeks database (via the `NIcalc` API in this workflow). Population monitoring and status reporting for lynx are coordinated by [Rovdata](https://rovdata.no/Gaupe.aspx), which publishes national and regional information based on the national monitoring programme for large carnivores. For example, the 2025 status report gives a national population estimate expressed as a range and relates this to counts of family groups of lynx [@rovdata_gaupe_status_2025]. 3. **Interpretation**: An indicator value of 1 means that the lynx population in the reporting unit is at least as large as expected under the reference condition used in Naturindeksen. Values decreasing toward zero indicate that the population index is further below that reference. 4. **Results and development needs**: For the current reporting period (2020-2024) the national indicator value is 0.13, with the highest value for region South (0.20), the lowest value for region West (0.00). The national indicator has been relatively stable fluctuating between 0.09 and 0.13 with a similar trend for all the regions. Region West has been at a minimum since 1990. There are no specific development needs, except for a possible review of reference values and the scaling function.
indikatorenhet: The unit of the raw data is the number of family groups of lynx.
innsamlingsmetode: [Rovdata](https://rovdata.no/Gaupe.aspx) is responsible for monitoring lynx in Norway and for maintaining an overview of how many lynx there are in the country. The status pages report population status using family groups of lynx and national/regional targets set by the Storting [@rovdata_gaupe_status_2025].
dekket_tidsperiode: Indicator values are available for the assessment years in Naturindeksen: 2000, 2010, 2014, 2019, and 2024. To produce indicator estimates for these years, input is combined over a short window (typically two to three years), as specified in the Naturindeks indicator protocol. Spatially, data are organised by the eight large-carnivore management regions (_forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt_, regions 1–8). Rovdata publishes status by these regions, including national targets for annual family groups of lynx per region [@rovdata_gaupe_status_2025]. In Naturindeksen, indicator and reference values are stored at management-region scale (IC units), then aggregated to five geographic regions and national level for reporting.
radata: Population monitoring and status information are accessible at [Rovdata](https://rovdata.no/Gaupe.aspx) and the relevant status pages [@rovdata_gaupe_status_2025]. Methodological documentation for the indicator: [Naturindeksen – gaupe](https://naturindeks.no/Indicators/gaupe).
arealrepresentativitet: Following the metadata pathway Aggregate (population model, large-carnivore management region) – [Scale – Truncate] – Downscale (municipalities) – Aggregate (geographic region) – Aggregate (national level): population estimates or indices are available per forvaltningsregion for rovvilt (IC unit in Naturindeksen). Each unit is normalised against _X~0~_ and _X~100~_ for that region (linear scaling with truncation to [0, 1]). Because rovvilt regions and the five Naturindeks geographic regions are two non-aligned partitions of Norway, we use municipalities (`BSunits`) as a common basic spatial unit. We assign the (scaled) rovvilt-region value to each municipality belonging to that region (uniform-value assumption), hereafter referred to as downscaling. Forest area (`Skog`) is used as the aggregation weight because lynx is a forest-associated species.
referansetilstand: The reference condition for the Eurasian lynx represents the natural population state that occurs in the absence of significant human influence. In this state, population dynamics and size are regulated by natural processes – primarily prey availability. The lynx fulfils a vital functional role in Norwegian forest ecosystems as a specialised predator of roe deer, but it is a highly adaptable hunter that incorporates hares as a significant secondary prey source. By exerting top-down control, the lynx influences not only prey numbers but also their behaviour, distribution, and vigilance.
referanseverdier: _X~100~_ is set per large-carnivore management region (IC unit in Naturindeksen), using suitable area and density within each _rovviltregion_ and expert assessment: it represents the expected lynx population (or equivalent index) under reference conditions in that unit. _X~0~_ is defined as no lynx in the unit (functional absence).
annen_informasjon: Reference levels are held fixed in this workflow (their own uncertainties are not propagated). Regional and national values are area-weighted summaries of forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt, so they inherit model uncertainty at management-region scale and any mismatch between administrative regions and ecological variation within the five Naturindeks geographic regions. Monitoring design and sample effort differ between species and regions; uneven coverage can affect the population models that enter Naturindeksen.
pavirkningsfaktorer: Natural regulation of Norway's Eurasian lynx population is primarily driven by prey availability, particularly roe deer, alongside intraspecific social mechanisms such as territoriality. However, these natural constraints are often superseded by anthropogenic factors, specifically a management policy that classifies the lynx as a game species subject to legal hunting quotas (licence hunting) to mitigate conflicts over high levels of livestock depredation. Furthermore, the overall population size is influenced by illegal killing.

precision: Approximate 95% Monte Carlo interval (2.5th–97.5th percentile of 1000 resampled area-weighted means) as inferential uncertainty around the point estimate (median).

beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: This indicator represents the proportion of productive forest area with more than two vertical tree layers (multi-layered forests). In forests shaped by natural disturbances and succession, a substantial part of the forest will be multi-layered. Stand-replacing disturbances that occur at certain intervals, might however result in one tree layer characterzing the forest. Modern even-aged forestry practices will result in one tree layer for much of the managed forest. Multi-layered forests will generally have more varied habitats and resources for species than one-layered forests. This indicator has been proposed as a voluntary indicator in EU. 2. **Methods**: Data for this indicator comes from the National Forest Inventory (NFI), where the number of tree layers around 0.1 ha of the NFI plot has been recorded for productive forest by current methods since the mid-1990s [@viken2025-feltinstruks]. 3. **Interpretation**: The non-scaled indicator is the area-weighted proportion of productive forest land that is categorized to multilayered (`flersjiktet`). The indicator is scaled for each county/sub-county with _X~0~_ = 0% multilayered forest and _X~100~_-values corresponding to the proportion expected under reference condition. Regional and national scaled values are area-weighted means of scaled county/sub-county values. 4. **Results and development needs**: The indicator value for the current reporting period (2020-2024) is 0.91, and has increased since 2010 (2010-2014: 0.86, 2015-2019: 0.90). The lowest value is in the region Vest (0.75) and the higest value in the region South (0.96). The indicator should not be used at finer spatial resolution than allows reliable estimates. We suggest using counties for this indicator. There are no specific development needs for the indicator measure from the NFI data. However, a more thorough analysis and review of the assessment of reference values and the scaling function is needed.
indikatorenhet: The indicator is specified as the area-weighted proportion (%) of productive forest area with more than two vertical tree layers (`best_form` = 3), relative to the total productive forest area.
innsamlingsmetode: There are about 12 000 NFI plots in forest ecosystems, distributed on a regular grid, with varying grid density for forest below/above the coniferous forest line and in Finnmark county. All NFI plots are sampled over a 5-year period, with a representative sampling scheme every year, allowing unbiased estimates from data for each year. Stands are classified as single-layered, two-layered, or multi-layered. A single-layered stand consists predominantly of trees in one canopy layer. A two-layered stand consists of two distinct canopy layers representing different stand development stages. The lower layer must contain viable trees to form a stand if the upper layer is removed. A multi-layered stand contains three or more canopy layers, with continuous variation in tree age and size. After removal of the upper canopy, the remaining trees should still constitute a two- or multi-layered stand. Tree layers are described in the variable `best_form` extracted from the NFI data. It iscategorical and the multi-layered category states that the forest has trees in more than two vertical layers, where tree-age variation also is a characteristic of the stand.
dekket_tidsperiode: Data are available from the mid-1990s, when current recording methods were established. Annual estimates are possible due to representative sampling every year. For this indicator all data from each full inventory cycle of 5 years are used, starting in 2010. The data are representative for all productive forest land within the selected region. Spatial resolution should be limited to the resolution allowing for reliable estimates, probably counties.
radata: The data used for this indicator have been made available by the Norwegian National Forest Inventory under a specific data use agreement of 2025-10-20, between NIBIO and the specified users. Further use of these data requires a separate data user agreement with NIBIO.
arealrepresentativitet: The spatial aggregation pathway is Aggregate (NFI plots to county) – [Scale – Truncate] – Aggregate (geographic region) – Aggregate (national level). For each NFI plot we derive weighted numerator and denominator areas from `best_form`, where multi-layered plots (`best_form` = 3) contribute to the numerator and all productive forest land (`arealtype` = 1) contribute to the denominator. Non-scaled indicator values for each reporting period are then calculated separately for counties, regions, and the national level as the area-weighted share: sum of numerator area divided by sum of denominator area. Scaling and truncation are applied after county/sub-county aggregation: each unit is normalised with _X~0~_ = 0 and a county/sub-county-specific _X~100~_ @sec-reference-levels using a linear function, and values above 1 are truncated to 1. Regional and national scaled values are area-weighted means of already scaled county/sub-county values. The indicator should not be used at finer spatial resolution than allows reliable estimates. We suggest using counties.
referansetilstand: The reference condition is considered to be intact forest ecosystems, where effects of human activities are clearly subordinate to those of natural ecosystem processes and disturbances.
referanseverdier: NA
annen_informasjon: Uncertainties relate to the variability in the frequency of forest layers among NFI plots and assessment errors for tree layers within NFI plots. This uncertainty is quantified by bootstrapping; the results report the resulting uncertainty for scaled values. There will also be uncertainty related to the setting of the upper reference value and to the shape of the relationship between indicator values and ecosystem condition. These uncertainties are not quantified.
pavirkningsfaktorer: Natural disturbances and succession at small scale or with moderate severity will generally result in multi-layered forests. Severe, stand-replacing disturbances may result in one-layered forests, but such disturbances are expected to be rare. Modern even-aged forestry practices will result in one tree layer for much of the managed forest.
version_comment: County/sub-county reference scaling (X0 = 0%, X100 varies by unit); scaled regional/national bootstrap
precision: Approximate 95% bootstrap interval (2.5th–97.5th percentile of 1000 bootstrap draws) as inferential uncertainty around the point estimate (median). At county or sub-county level, bootstrapping is applied directly to NFI plot data; at regional and national level, uncertainty is propagated from scaled county bootstrap draws.

beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: The moose (*Alces alces*) is the largest ungulate found in forest ecosystems in Norway. Through browsing on tree saplings and shrubs, particularly pine, rowan and willow, moose exert a strong influence on tree regeneration, forest structure and plant biodiversity, and as a large prey animal form a central component of the prey base for apex predators [@niedzialkowska2022_moose; @rodgers2025_moose]. In the period with reasonably good overview of cervid densities in Norway (about the last 200 years), populations have been strongly influenced by human activity. In many areas, moose densities have historically exceeded, and in some areas continue to exceed, the reference condition, resulting in impacts on forest regeneration and vegetation composition. 2. **Methods**: The moose indicator (elg) expresses population density as number of individuals per km² below the climatic tree line, reported at county level, as described on [Naturindeksen – elg](https://naturindeks.no/Indicators/elg). Underlying population information for moose in Norway is linked to the national monitoring programme for cervids, which has operated since 1991 and is owned by Landbruksdirektoratet and run by NINA [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. Much of the monitoring material is collected from animals harvested during hunting (for example jaw bones, slaughter weight, and for moose also reproductive organs from females) [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. The reference condition is an expert-assessed state in which moose occur throughout suitable forest habitat under current climate conditions, with natural, non-managed predator regimes, and in the absence of forest management . Estimated densities by county are normalised using a unimodal scaling function. Scaled county values are aggregated to five geographic regions and national level. 3. **Interpretation**: An indicator value of 1 means that moose abundance in the reporting unit is as large as expected under the reference condition. Values <1 indicate that the density is either lower or higher than the reference value. 4. **Results and development needs**: For the current reporting period (2020-2024) the national indicator value is 0.54, with a much higher value for region South (0.77) and an extremely low value for region West (0.00). The national indicator value has increased from 0.39 in 1990. Trends for values in different regions have varied between regions and periods. There are no specific development needs, except for a possible review of reference values and the scaling function.
indikatorenhet: The moose abundance is expressed as number of individuals per km².
innsamlingsmetode: The national monitoring programme for cervids collects most material from harvested animals during hunting seasons [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. For moose, samples can include lower jaw and slaughter weight, and reproductive organs (egg stalks) from females [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. Further methodological details are given on [Naturindeksen – elg](https://naturindeks.no/Indicators/elg).
dekket_tidsperiode: The underlying data are collected annually. Indicator values are available for the assessment years in Naturindeksen: 1990, 2000, 2010, 2014, 2019, and 2024. To produce indicator estimates for these years, input is typically combined over a short window (typically two to three years). Spatially, data and indicator values are handled at county level, then aggregated to five geographic regions and national level for reporting.
radata: The underlying data on hunting statistics are available upon request from Hjorteviltregisteret [@hjorteviltregisteret]. However, these data must be combined with data on demographic variables and other parameters to calculate the density of moose per county, as described [here](https://naturindeks.nina.no/docs/1c2b2f52-4d91-4563-b65d-b9813798dd06.pdf). The resulting data for the density of moose can be accessed directly and used in calculating scaled indicator values as described in sections 7 and 9 below. Indicator values from the Norwegian Nature Index can be found in @nater_ni2025_2025. Indicator values, variable values and reference values can be downloaded from the Nature Index database using the API, as I have done below. The data is licenced under CC-BY 4.0.
arealrepresentativitet: Following the metadata pathway Aggregate (population model, county level) – [Scale – Truncate] – Aggregate (regional/national level): population density estimates are available per county. Each county value is normalised with a unimodal scaling function (optimum at _X~100~_; lower and upper reference values for very deteriorated condition at _X~0~_ and _X~0h~_; see @sec-reference-levels). Regional (east, south, west, central, north) and national indicator values are then obtained as area-weighted combinations of the scaled county values.
referansetilstand: The species-specific reference condition for moose represents the natural population state occurring in the absence of significant human influence, where population size, structure and dynamics are regulated primarily by natural processes – including predation by natural carnivore communities, particularly wolves, food availability, and habitat carrying capacity under natural vegetation conditions. The population fulfills its natural functional role as the dominant large herbivore in forest ecosystems, exerting strong influence on tree regeneration, forest structure and plant biodiversity through browsing on tree saplings and shrubs – particularly pine, rowan and willow – at naturally occurring intensities, and forming a central prey base for apex predators. Population size naturally varies within dynamic ranges in response to climatic variation, natural disturbance regimes, and ecological interactions with other herbivores such as red deer and roe deer.
referanseverdier: NA
annen_informasjon: Reference levels are held fixed in this workflow (their own uncertainties are not propagated). Regional and national values are area-weighted average indicator values for included counties, so they inherit both model uncertainty at county level and any mismatch between county boundaries and ecological variation within regions.
pavirkningsfaktorer: One of the major natural impact factors is variation in weather conditions, especially temperature during reproduction and snow conditions in winter, affecting food quality and availability, recruitment and survival. Predation from large carnivores and disease and parasites are other key factors affecting survival. Major anthropogenic impact factors are land use change, traffic accidents, hunting, strong limitation of large carnivore populations, and climate change.
version_comment: First version on ecRxiv; indicator described in the Norwegian Nature Index
precision: Uncertainties around the estimated true value reported as probability distributions and confidence intervals.

Why is this relevant for describing ecosystem condition in this ecosystem? What are the main anthropogenic impact factors? --> Small rodents, such as lemmings and mice, are keystone species in alpine ecosystems. They function as a trophic link between the primary producers and top predators. When population are high, they impose a large disturbance on the vegetation, but at the same time they fuel the higher trophic levels and ensure survival and breeding success for species like raptors and foxes. Rodent cycles have a frequency of about 3-4 years, and it is the amplitude (size or height) of these peaks that make up this indicator. Rodent cycles, both their regularity and their amplitude, are negatively affected by many known and unknown drivers. The most important anthropogenic driver is climate change, with warmer and wetter winters causing rodent declines due to the effect that this has on the snow cover. 2. **Methods**: <!-- What kind of data is used? How is the data customized (modified, estimated, integrated) to fit its purpose as an indicator? --> Rodent numbers have been monitored from 1990 to 2020 using traps. A new national monitoring program was initiated in 2020 based on camera traps, but these data are not yet integrated with the existing time series, so the 2024 estimate is based on expert opinion, informed by various data sources. We get the data from the Norwegian Nature Index database [@nater_naturindeks_2025] where also the X~100~ reference values are stored. These represent the predicted mean number of rodents in peaks year over a 10 year period, given minimal anthropogenic influence. The reference values are also based on expert opinion, but informed by extensive empirical data. 3. **Interpretation**: <!-- Add a very short description of how the indicator values should be interpreted. Here's an example for a bumblebee indicator: An indicator value of 1 signifies an intact bumblebee community. Values decreasing toward zero reflect negative ecological change, specifically the decline of species expected to be present. This metric does not account for potentially positive changes, such as increases in species' abundance or the arrival of new species. Tip: Add text on the line directly following the subheader, and don't introduce blank lines. This way the whole paragraph renders as a block quote. --> An indicator value of 1 means that rodent numbers in peak years are as numerous, or more than what we expect under the reference condition. Values decreasing toward zero indicates that the average rodent peaks are diminishing. 4. **Results and development needs**: <!-- Briefly, what does the indicator say about the ecosystem condition. What is the current status of the metric (can it be used or is it still in development), and what immediate tasks remain to improve the indicator or to make the indicator operational --> The indicator value for Norway as a whole in 2024 was 0.28 [95% CI = 0.26-0.30]. This is extremely low and reflects the deminishing effect of rodent cycles on Norwegian alpine ecosystems. Development needs include an integration of the current monitoring time series, with the old time series based on trap monitoring.

beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: The roe deer (*Capreolus capreolus*) is a small ungulate found in forest ecosystems in Norway. Through selective browsing on forbs, herbs and shrubs, roe deer influence understory plant biodiversity and vegetation composition, and as a prey animal also contribute to supporting populations of apex predators [@lorenzini2022_roedeer; @hewison2025_roedeer]. In the period with reasonably good overview of cervid densities in Norway (about the last 200 years), populations have been strongly influenced by human activity, including hunting, varying levels of control of large predators, and changes in land use and climate. 2. **Methods**: The roe deer abundance indicator expresses population density as number of individuals per km² below the climatic tree line, reported at county level, as described on [Naturindeksen – rådyr](https://naturindeks.no/Indicators/raadyr). Underlying population information for roe deer in Norway is linked to the national monitoring programme for cervids, which has operated since 1991 and is owned by Landbruksdirektoratet and run by NINA [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. Much of the monitoring material is collected from animals harvested during hunting (for example lower jaw and slaughter weight) [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. The reference condition is an expert-assessed state in which roe deer may occur in suitable forest habitat under current climate conditions, with natural, non-managed predator regimes, and in the absence of forest management. Impacts on other biodiversity are considered as less pronounced for this species than for larger cervids. Estimated densities by county are normalised using a unimodal scaling function. Scaled county values are aggregated to five geographic regions and national level. 3. **Interpretation**: An indicator value of 1 means that roe deer abundance in the reporting unit is as large as expected under the reference condition. Values <1 indicate that the density is either lower or higher than the reference value. 4. **Results and development needs**: For the current reporting period (2020-2024) the national indicator value is 0.19, with very low values for regions East (0.07), West (0.02) and North (0,00). The national indicator value has decreased somewhat from 0.23 in 1990. Values for the regions have varied or been rather stable, except for a consistent decline since 2000 for region Central. There are no specific development needs, except for a possible review of reference values and the scaling function.
indikatorenhet: The roe deer abundance is expressed as number of individuals per km².
innsamlingsmetode: The national monitoring programme for cervids collects most material from harvested animals during hunting seasons [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. For roe deer, samples can include lower jaw and slaughter weight [@hjortevilt_nasjonal_overvaking]. Further methodological details are given on [Naturindeksen – rådyr](https://naturindeks.no/Indicators/raadyr).
dekket_tidsperiode: The underlying data are collected annually. Indicator values are available for the assessment years in Naturindeksen: 1990, 2000, 2010, 2014, 2019, and 2024. To produce indicator estimates for these years, input is typically combined over a short window (typically two to three years). Spatially, data and indicator values are handled at county level, then aggregated to five geographic regions and national level for reporting.
radata: The underlying data on hunting statistics are available upon request from Hjorteviltregisteret [@hjorteviltregisteret]. However, these data must be combined with data on demographic variables and other parameters to calculate the density of moose per county, as described [here](https://naturindeks.nina.no/docs/1c2b2f52-4d91-4563-b65d-b9813798dd06.pdf). The resulting data for the density of moose can be accessed directly and used in calculating scaled indicator values as described in sections 7 and 9 below. Indicator values from the Norwegian Nature Index can be found in @nater_ni2025_2025. Indicator values, variable values and reference values can be downloaded from the Nature Index database using the API, as I have done below. The data is licenced under CC-BY 4.0.
arealrepresentativitet: Following the metadata pathway Aggregate (population model, county level) – [Scale – Truncate] – Aggregate (regional/national level): population density estimates are available per county. Each county value is normalised with a unimodal scaling function (optimum at _X~100~_; lower and upper reference values for very deteriorated condition at _X~0~_ and _X~0h~_; see @sec-reference-levels). Regional (east, south, west, central, north) and national indicator values are then obtained as area-weighted combinations of the scaled county values.
referansetilstand: The reference condition for roe deer represents the natural population state occurring in the absence of significant human influence, where population size, structure and dynamics are regulated primarily by natural processes – including predation by natural carnivore communities, food availability, snow depth and habitat carrying capacity under natural vegetation conditions. The population fulfills its natural functional role as a selective browser in forest ecosystems, influencing understory plant biodiversity and vegetation composition through selective browsing on forbs, herbs and shrubs at naturally occurring intensities, and contributing to the prey base of apex predators. Population size naturally varies within dynamic ranges in response to climatic variation including winter snow conditions, natural disturbance regimes, and ecological interactions with other herbivores such as red deer and moose.
referanseverdier: NA
annen_informasjon: Reference levels are held fixed in this workflow (their own uncertainties are not propagated). Regional and national values are area-weighted summaries of counties, so they inherit both model uncertainty at county scale and any mismatch between county boundaries and ecological variation within regions.
pavirkningsfaktorer: One of the major natural impact factors is variation in weather conditions, especially temperature during reproduction and snow conditions in winter, affecting food quality and availability, recruitment and survival. Predation from large carnivores and disease and parasites are other key factors affecting survival. Major anthropogenic impact factors are land use change, traffic accidents, hunting, strong limitation of large carnivore populations, and climate change.
version_comment: First version on ecRxiv; indicator described in the Norwegian Nature Index
precision: Uncertainties around the estimated true value reported as probability distributions and confidence intervals.

beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: Rowan (*Sorbus aucuparia*), aspen (*Populus tremula*) and goat willow (*Salix caprea*) (collectively abbreviated ROS) are boreal tree species which represent important substrate, habitat or food sources for many fungi, lichens, bryophytes, and animals. Under natural forest conditions these tree species favour disturbances like floods, fires and storms with ensuing succession to provide openings in the forest and avoid competition from dense spruce forest. The aggregated volume per hectare of ROS species is considered to be positively associated with ecosystem condition. Data for this indicator come from the National Forest Inventory (NFI), where the volume of ROS species for trees >10 cm diameter at breast-height has been recorded for each NFI plot since 1994. The recorded mean volume of ROS species is compared to reference values for regions, based on expert assessments. 2. **Methods**: For each NFI plot, the combined volume of rowan, aspen and goat willow is taken from the NFIvariable `ROS_10_PRHA` (m³ ha⁻¹). Results are calculated for sequential 5-year periods from 2010 and aggregated with area weights to county or sub-county, regional and national units. The value for each county or sub-county is scaled against its specific reference level before regional and national values are calculated as area-weighted means of scaled county values. 3. **Interpretation**: An indicator value of 1 implies that the ROS volume is at least as high as expected in the reference condition. Values decreasing toward zero reflect lower combined volume of rowan, aspen and goat willow relative to the reference. 4. **Results and development needs**: For the current reporting period (2020-2024) the national indicator value is 0.45 (95% CI: 0.41 - 0.49). The regional indicator values range from 0.34 - 0.67, with the East having the lowest value and the South having the highest value. The indicator values increase over time nationally and for all regions. There are no specific development needs for the indicator measure. However more thorough analyses and review of the assessment of reference values and the scaling function is needed.
indikatorenhet: The indicator is specified as combined standing volume per hectare (m³ ha⁻¹) for rowan, aspen and goat willow on the NFI plot (`ROS_10_PRHA`).
innsamlingsmetode: There are about 12 000 NFI plots in forest ecosystems, distributed on a regular grid, with varying grid density for forest below/above the coniferous forest line and in Finnmark county [@viken2025-feltinstruks]. In each NFI plot, all individual trees with a diameter ≥5 cm at breast height are determined to species and measured for several variables, including diameter at breast height. From the data, the volume of individual trees are calculated. For this indicator, we use the combined volume per hectare of trees of rowan, aspen, and goat willow with a diameter at breast height of at least 10 cm. All NFI plots are sampled over a 5-year period, with a representative sampling scheme every year, allowing unbiased estimates from data for each year.
dekket_tidsperiode: Data are available from 2010, when NFI had extended the grid to all forest land. Annual estimates are possible due to representative sampling every year. For this indicator all data from each full inventory cycle of 5 years are used, starting in 2010. Spatial resolution should be limited to the resolution applied to reference values, that is counties or sub-county units for scaling and regions for aggregated reporting.
radata: The data used for this indicator have been made available by the Norwegian National Forest Inventory under a specific data use agreement of 2026-05-29, between NIBIO and the specified users. Further use of the data requires a separate data user agreement with NIBIO
arealrepresentativitet: The spatial aggregation pathway is Aggregate (NFI plots to county/sub-county) – [Scale – Truncate] – Aggregate (geographic region) – Aggregate (national level). For each NFI plot we create `indicator_continuous_weighted = ros_10_prha * au_areal`. Non-scaled indicator values for each reporting period are calculated separately for each geographic unit as area-weighted arithmetic means of all NFI plots within that unit: sum of `indicator_continuous_weighted` divided by sum of `au_areal`. This is done for counties or sub-counties, regions, and at national level. Scaling and truncation are applied only after the non-scaled county or sub-county aggregates have been calculated: each county or sub-county is scaled against its own lower reference level _X~0~_ (0 m³ ha⁻¹) and upper reference level _X~100~_ using a linear scaling function, and values above 1 are truncated to 1 at that step. Regional and national scaled point estimates are area-weighted means of the already scaled county or sub-county values, using each county or sub-county's represented area as weight. Non-scaled regional and national point estimates are still calculated directly from all plots within each region or the whole country.
referansetilstand: The reference condition is considered to be intact forest ecosystems where effects of human activities are clearly subordinate to those of natural ecosystem processes and disturbances.
referanseverdier: The lower reference level _X~0~_ is set to 0 m³ ha⁻¹ and the upper reference level _X~100~_ is set separately for each county or sub-county. X0 denotes the worst possible condition and X100 denotes the best possible condition on the original volume scale. Between _X~0~_ and _X~100~_, indicator values are scaled linearly to a 0-1 indicator scale. Scaled values above 1 are truncated to 1 when volume exceeds the county-specific X100. The county and sub-county _X~100~_ values used in the analyses are listed in @tbl-rose-reference-values. _X~0~_ is 0 m³ ha⁻¹ for all units.
annen_informasjon: Reference levels are held fixed in this workflow (their own uncertainties are not propagated). Regional and national values are area-weighted summaries of counties, so they inherit both model uncertainty at county level and any mismatch between county boundaries and ecological variation within regions.
pavirkningsfaktorer: Natural disturbances such as fires, floods, or windthrows are important to maintain site conditions for recruitment of rowan, aspen, and goat willows (ROS). Human impacts with negative effects on ROS species are linked to forestry activities, especially clear-cutting, dense planting, other forest management, and fire prevention, although clearcuts may also open the forest for increased recruitment of ROS species. Human management resulting in high abundances of livestock or wild ungulates will negatively affect recruitment of ROS species. Human management of ground conditions, other tree species and animal browsing may also directly facilitate recruitment and growth of ROS species. See @solberg2011_ros.
version_comment: Initial version
precision: Approximate 95% bootstrap interval (2.5th–97.5th percentile of 1000 bootstrap draws) as inferential uncertainty around the point estimate (median). At county or sub-county level, bootstrapping is applied directly to NFI plot data; at regional and national level, uncertainty is propagated from scaled county bootstrap draws.

beskrivelse: <!--# With a maximum of 300 words, describe the indicator in general terms as you would to a non-expert. Think of this as a kind of common language summary. Follow the four numbers sub-headers below. under point 2, it is possible under include a bullet point list of the specific steps in the workflow. --> 1. **Background and rationale**: Atlantic salmon (*Salmo salar*) is a keystone species in Norwegian rivers. Salmons are andromous fish, meaning that they migrate between freshwater, where they spawn, and saltwater. Salmon stock size is thus affected by natural conditions and anthropogenic impacts both in freshwater and at sea. The most important negative impacts are salmon farming, climate change, hydromorphological changes, alien species, acid precipitation, and contaminants. <!-- What does the metric represent? Why is this relevant for describing ecosystem condition in this ecosystem? What are the main anthropogenic impact factors? --> 2. **Methods**: Wild stocks of salmon in Norway are classified according to a so-called "[quality norm](#norm)", which evaluates the status of salmon stocks in two dimensions ([VRL 2011](#vrl11)), viz. population status and genetic integrity. The overall stock quality is determined by the poorest of the two dimensions. A comprehensive classification of salmon stocks is published every fifth year by the [Norwegian Scientific Advisory Committee for Atlantic Salmon](https://vitenskapsradet.no/). The indicator is defined in line with the quality norm and the published assessments, but it is turned into a continuous score using the approach defined by the [Water Framework Directive](#wfd). The workflow thus consists of the following steps: * Variables that are available on an annual basis are averaged for each accounting period. * Remaining variables are taken from the most recently published assessment. * Uncertain or missing values are filled in using a re-sampling procedure. * The underlying variables are transformed into continuous "normalised Ecological Quality Ratios" (nEQR) between 0 and 1 using the reference levels defined by the quality norm. * The population status for each river is calculated by an additive combination of the nEQR values for the attainment of the conservation limit and for the harvest potential. * The indicator value for each river is calculated by combining the nEQR values for population status and genetic integrity using the one-out--all-out principle. * The indicator values are aggregated spatially to obtain national or regional averages. <!-- What kind of data is used? How is the data customized (modified, estimated, integrated) to fit its purpose as an indicator? --> 3. **Interpretation**: An indicator value of 1 signifies a condition where the wild salmon stock has a productivity that corresponds to undisturbed conditions, where its at-sea survival ensures a normal harvest level, and where the stock is not genetically affected by escaped farmed salmons. Values decreasing toward zero reflect that at least one of these conditions is met to a lesser degree. <!-- Add a very short description of how the indicator values should be interpreted. Here's an example for a bumblebee indicator: An indicator value of 1 signifies an intact bumblebee community. Values decreasing toward zero reflect negative ecological change, specifically the decline of species expected to be present. This metric does not account for potentially positive changes, such as increases in species' abundance or the arrival of new species. Tip: Add text on the line directly following the subheader, and don't introduce blank lines. This way the whole paragraph renders as a block quote. --> 4. **Results and development needs**: The indicator is ready for use. Its values for 2024 mean that salmon stock quality is poor. <!-- Briefly, what does the indicator say about the ecosystem condition. What is the current status of the metric (can it be used or is it still in development), and what immediate tasks remain to improve the indicator or to make the indicator operational -->
indikatorenhet: According to the quality norm, salmon stock quality is reported as a categorical score with five levels: "high", "good", "moderate", "poor", "bad". (The Norwegian terms for the five quality categories are *svært god*, *god*, *moderat*, *dårlig*, and *svært dårlig*. The verbatim translations of these terms would be "very good", "good", "moderate", "bad", and "very bad", respectively. Here, however, the categories are translated as "*high*", "good", "moderate", "*poor*", and "*bad*", respectively, because these are the established terms used in the [Water Framework Directive](#wfd).) The stock quality score is obtained by combining the partial scores for the two criteria ("subnorms") of the quality norm: (1) The (a) attainment of the conservation limit and (b) harvest potential are both expressed as *percentages*. The categorisation is accomplished with three different conversion tables, depending on the absolute spawning stock size (see [quality norm](#norm), App. II). (2) Genetic integrity is expressed in terms of a categorical score with four levels: "high", "moderate", "poor", "bad". ("Good" is not used as a separate score by the relevant subcriterion. Although the highest score is referred to as "good/high", it coincides with the reference condition, i.e. the absence of any observable genetic impact from farmed salmon; it is therefore here treated as "high".) The two scores obtained are combined using the one-out--all-out principle, i.e. the poorer of the two partial scores determines the overall score. The simplified procedure reports stock quality as a categorical score with three levels: "good/high", "moderate" and "poor/bad". <!--# What are the original units for the most relevant variables in the data-->
innsamlingsmetode: Most relevant salmon rivers are included in the dataset, i.e. all river systems in which significant salmon stocks spawn today or have spawned historically. The salmon rivers with the largest spawning stocks are assessed regularly using the methodology described in the quality norm (currently, *N* ≈ 180). Additional salmon rivers are assessed using a simplified procedure (*N* ≈ 260). Some smaller salmon rivers, most of which have only few spawning individuals, are not included in the dataset. <!-- How was the data sampled? Describe potential sampling biases -->
dekket_tidsperiode: The **spatial** resolution of this indicator is on the level of *river systems* (Norw. *vassdrag*), specifically their anadromous proportion (i.e., the part of a river system which is accessible to salmons). The **temporal** resolution of the quality norm for salmon is *five years*. However, some of the components of the indicator are estimated and updated annually for large/important rivers systems. This applies to the attainment of the conservation limit and the harvest potential. <!--# Describe the temporal and spatial resolution and extent of the data used -->
radata: All data related to the quality norm and simplified procedure are publicly available but not machine-readable. They can be accessed by downloading the reports published by VRL (see [list of publications](https://www.vitenskapsradet.no/Rapporter), in Norwegian) and should be referred to by citing the specific report(s) used. Annual data on selected variables have been and can be obtained by contacting the leader or secretariat of the Committee (see [contact details](https://www.vitenskapsradet.no/Om-VRL/Kontakt)). <!--# Is the data openly available? If not, how can one access it? What are the key references to the datasets? -->
arealrepresentativitet: The aggregation pathway used here has the following steps: 1. *Scaling.* The variable values are linearly scaled so that X~0~ becomes 0 and X~100~ becomes 1. Note that the resulting values may be larger than 1 (if X > X~100~). 2. *Temporal aggregration.* The scaled values are aggregated temporally by calculating an arithmetic average for the years in each three-year accounting period. 3. *Transformation.* The temporally aggregated values are transformed in a stepwise-linear manner in accordance with the [reference levels](#reference-levels). 4. *Thematic aggregration.* The transformed values of the attainment of the conservation limit and of the harvest potential are aggregated by combining them additively into an indicator of population status. Population status and genetic integrity are then aggregated by applying the one-out--all-out principle. 5. *Truncation.* If indicator values are larger than 1, they are truncated to 1. 6. *Spatial aggregration.* Indicator values for the specific river systems are spatially aggregated using size-weighted arithmetic averages across all relevant water bodies (where "size" is the total *anadromous length* of the river system). <!-- Describe in word the same aggregation pathway presented in the metadata.xlsx. If you have scaled against the reference value, it is especially important to know if you did any avergaing or summations etc. beforehand. An example text for a rather simple case could be: "The variable is scaled at the initial polygon level and the point estimate is a area-weighted arithmetic mean of all polygins. There is no transformation, and truncation is not needed as the indicator becomes naturally bound between 0 and 1". -->
referansetilstand: According to the [quality norm](#norm), a salmon stock is in the reference condition if it fulfils all of the following three conditions: 1. The *cumulative biomass of adult females* equals the conservation limit, which is "the amount of female salmons, measured in terms of weight, that has to spawn in order for the optimal number of smolt to be able to leave the river each year." The "optimal number of smolt" (which are young salmons that are ready to migrate towards the sea) means the number under undisturbed conditions. 2. The *harvest potential* equals the normal harvest level, which is "the level of harvest that the stock shall be able to sustain in a given year based on knowledge of natural survival at sea, and given that the stock at the same time reaches the conservation limit." Here, "natural survival at sea" means that the survival in the marine phase is unaffected by human activity. 3. The stock is not *genetically affected* by escaped farmed salmons (or other anthropogenic activity such as selective harvesting). Note that the term "conservation limit" (Norw. *gytebestandsmål*, verbatim "target spawning stock"), contrary to a possible connotation of "conservation", is not a political target but is estimated based on available empirical evidence alone (see [Forseth et al. 2013](#for13)). <!--# Define the reference condition (or refer to where it is defined). Note the distinction between reference condition and reference levels 10.3897/oneeco.5.e58216 -->
referanseverdier: If one follows the procedure applied by the [Water Framework Directive](#wfd), the quality categories can be used to define reference levels for X~0~, X~20~, X~40~, X~60~, X~80~, and X~100~. The reference levels then follow from the [quality norm](#norm) (App. II and III) and need to be applied separately to its (sub)criteria: * For attainment of the conservation limit, there are three sets of reference levels, depending on the absolute size of the spawning population, delineating five categories ([quality norm](#norm), App. II-a): "bad" (X~0~ ≤ X ≤ X~20~), "poor" (X~20~ < X ≤ X~40~), "moderate" (X~40~ < X ≤ X~60~), "good" (X~60~ < X ≤ X~80~), and "high" (X~80~ < X ≤ X~100~). * For harvest potential, the reference levels are X~40~ = 60%, X~60~ = 80%, X~80~ = 90%, and X~100~ = 100% ([quality norm](#norm), App. II-b). * For genetic integrity, the categories can be represented as midpoints of the respective intervals, i.e. "bad" as 0.1, "poor" as 0.3, "moderate" as 0.5, and "high" as 0.9 (since "good" is not used). The combination of these partial indicator values into the final indicator values follows Appendices I and II of the quality norm. The quality norm (Art. 3) enforces the environmental *objective* that all stocks of salmon, with a few specified exceptions, shall have at least "good quality". According to the reference levels defined here, this amounts to the objective that X > X~60~). <!--# If relevant (i.e. if you have normalised a variable), describe the reference levels used to normalise the variable. Use the terminology where X~0~ refers to the reference level (the variable value) denoting the worst possible condition; X~100~denotes the optimum or best possible condition; and X~*n*~, where in is between 0 and 100, denotes any other anchoring points linking the variable scale to the indicator scale (e.g. the threshold value between good and bad condition X~60^). Why was the current option chosen and how were the reference levels quantified? If the reference values are calculated as part of the analyses further down, please repeat the main information here. -->
annen_informasjon: All empirical data utilised in the analyses are subject to *observation error*. Some underlying assumptions are also related to *sampling error*. For example, harvest potential is estimated as actual harvest divided by the "normal harvest level". Whereas the actual harvest level is subject to noise (i.e. observation error), the normal harvest level is a function of at-sea survival, which is normally unknown, so that the median harvest potential of rivers thought to be fully recruited is used as a proxy. No attempt is made to quantify these uncertainties, but they can be regarded as comparatively small for the salmon stocks that are assessed using the quality norm. However, salmon stocks that are assessed using the simplified procedure are more uncertain. This is visible from the fact that the simplified procedure does not distinguish between "good" and "high" status or between "poor" and "bad" status. In addition, data on genetic integrity are unavailable for most of the latter stocks. A further uncertainty is related to the most appropriate weighting of river systems. The relevant magnitude for weighting is the size of the anadromous part of each river system. Estimates of both anadromous area and anadromous length are available. However, whereas area should in principle be preferred, other river indicators are weighted by the lengths of the ecosystem assets (areas being currently unavailable). Therefore, to ensure compatibility with other river indicators, the current indicator is weighted by length, too. Anadromous lengths may be biased (i.e. overestimated) by long and narrow tributaries, however. These questions are as yet unexplored. <!--# Describe the main reasons why you might not trust 100% the final value to represent the given ecosystem characteristic for the give ecosystem type. What aspects of this condition metric are most sensitive to subjective decitions? Is the spatial sampling sufficient? Does the choice of modeling framework affect the values? Is the metric relevant do describe ecosystem condition for the give ecosystem type? -->
pavirkningsfaktorer: Impact factors negatively affecting wild salmon are, in approximate decreasing order of importance (current impact and risk for future damage): salmon farming (via spread of salmon lice *Lepeophtheirus salmonis*, escape of farmed salmons, and infections), climate change, hydromorphological changes (regulation of rivers and lakes), other infections (not related to fish farming), alien species (mainly pink salmon *Oncorhynchus gorbuscha* and salmon fluke *Gyrodactylus salaris*), acid precipitation, contaminants, and overharvesting ([VRL 2025](#vrl25), p. 115; cf. [Forseth et al. 2017](#for17)). <!--# Describe the main natural and anthropogenic factors that affecst the metric -->

beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: The 'Erosive disturbance' indicator describes to what degree an ecosystem is affected by human-caused disturbances, mainly linked to erosion from heavy vehicles or damage from intensive human use, based on the 'tungekjoretoy' and 'slitasje' variables registered in ANO monitoring sites. 2. **Methods**: The indicator uses data from the Norwegian ANO nature monitoring program. The indicator is one-sided as a lack of this kind of erosive disturbance obviously is not a problem. The reference condition is defined as an ecosystem without any erosive disturbance (applies to all types of ecosystems and all regions), and thus the reference threshold for scaling is set to 0 disturbance at a site. The reference level X~60~, i.e. the threshold between good and reduced ecological condition, as well as X~0~, are set on an expert-judgement basis: less than 1/16th of the area affected by both heavy vehicles and overuse represents good condition, and more than 1/2 of the area for one of heavy vehicles or overuse plus up to 1/2 of the area for the other represents X~0~ where the ecosystem for sure has transformed into something else (see also Nybø et al. 2023 for an implementation of this indicator for Norwegian wetland and open lowland ecosystems). 3. **Interpretation**: An indicator value of 1 signifies that the median amount of erosive disturbance across ANO localities for that ecosystem, is zero. Values decreasing toward zero means more of the ANO localities have physical signs of erosive disturbance. 4. **Results and development needs**: The indicator is well developed and argued, and is thus operational. The indicator values are consistently close to 1 for all regions. One way to improve this indicator is to increase the resolution that the variable is recorded at in the field. Today the variable is recorded on a very coarse four-step scale which hides a lot of information.
indikatorenhet: Data on erosive disturbance in both 7_TK and 7_SE in ANO are given on a coarse 4 step scale within a 250 m^2^ sample circle, indicating how much area is affected by either heavy vehicle or overuse erosion, where 0 = 0 cover, 1 = 0-1/16 cover, 2 = 1/16-1/2 cover, and 3 = 1/2-1 cover.
innsamlingsmetode: At every ANO site, the indicator variable is registered at up to 18 monitoring points, dependent on the ecosystem designation.
dekket_tidsperiode: The ANO monitoring data available now represent one cycle of sampling from 2019-2024 comprising ca. 1000 sites across Norway. ANO has no defined end date. 2025 is the first year of repeated sampling for about 20% of the approximately 1000 ANO sites for all of mainland Norway (i.e. the Ecosystem Accounting Area). Annual sampling is spatially representative, in principle allowing to compute area-representative estimates for single years but also multiple-yr-reporting periods. The indicator at hand is calculated based on the ANO data from 2020-2024.
radata: The ANO data are openly available at https://kartkatalog.miljodirektoratet.no/Dataset/Details/2054
arealrepresentativitet: The variable is scaled at the initial ANO-point level and the indicator estimate is an arithmetic mean of all ANO-points. There is no transformation, and truncation is not needed as the indicator becomes naturally bound between 0 and 1.
referansetilstand: In Norway, the reference condition for natural ecosystems has been one of largely intact ecosystems without large-scale human modifications (Nybø and Evju 2017). For semi-natural ecosystems, human influence is allowed, and indeed a prerequisite, but then in the sense of appropriate, stable and traditional land-use practices. Thus, in terms of erosion species, the reference condition is defined as an ecosystem without any erosion plant species.

beskrivelse: 1. **Background and rationale**: This indicator describes mean winter snow depth in Norwegian mountain ecosystems. Snow depth is a key physical characteristic of mountain ecosystems because it influences the length of the snow season, soil temperatures, freeze-thaw exposure, plant phenology, grazing access, hydrology, and the winter conditions experienced by alpine and subalpine species. Changes in snow depth are closely linked to climate change and can alter ecological processes even where land-use pressure is low. 2. **Methods**: The indicator is calculated from daily seNorge snow depth data. For each "winter year", snow depth is averaged over the period December of the previous year to May of the current year. The resulting winter mean raster is clipped to the Norwegian mountain area using a mountain mask. Mean snow depth is then calculated separately for five mountain regions: Nord-Norge, Midt-Norge, Østlandet, Vestlandet and Sørlandet. The workflow is: - retrieve daily snow depth data from seNorge for December of the previous year and January-May of the current year; - crop the data to the bounding box of the mountain mask to reduce processing time; - calculate the mean snow depth over the December-May winter period; - mask the raster to mountain areas; - calculate mean snow depth within each mountain region; - calculate region-specific reference values from the 1961–1990 baseline period and convert annual values to a normalised 0–1 condition score using piece-wise linear transformation; - summarise the indicator values across 5-year reporting period; - simulate probability distributions for each regional and reporting period; - propagate these uncertainties and produce a national estimate and probability distribution; - export result indicator values and distributions 3. **Interpretation**: A value of 1 indicates snow depth equal to or greater than the historical reference condition, while values below 1 indicate reduced snow depth relative to the reference period. Lower values indicate increasing departure from historical snow conditions and may reflect climate-driven reductions in winter snow accumulation. 4. **Results and development needs**: The indicator value for Norway as a whole and for the 2020-2024 reporting period was 0.89 [95%CI: 0.69-0-96], indicating mean snow depths have not deviated very much from what was observed during the reference period. Further development should evaluate the sensitivity of results to the choice of reference period and summary statistic (median versus mean), assess whether capping values at 1 is appropriate, and validate indicator behaviour against previous ecosystem-condition assessments and independent evidence of climate impacts on mountain ecosystems.
indikatorenhet: The underlying variable is snow depth measured in cm.
innsamlingsmetode: The data are modelled gridded climate data rather than field samples collected specifically for this indicator. The indicator therefore inherits uncertainties from the underlying meteorological observations, interpolation/model structure, elevation effects, and the density and distribution of weather stations. Uncertainty may be larger in remote mountain areas where observations are sparse, and in areas where local topography produces fine-scale snow variation that is not fully represented by the raster resolution.
dekket_tidsperiode: The snow depth data are gridded daily raster data covering Norway. In this workflow, daily values are aggregated to a winter-year mean for the period December-May. The first complete winter year in the analysis is 1959, because this uses December 1958 and January-May 1959. The current script is set up to process winter years 1959-2026, depending on data availability from seNorge. Spatially, the analysis is restricted to modelled mountain areas in Norway. Final indicator values are reported for five broad regions: Nord-Norge, Midt-Norge, Østlandet, Vestlandet and Sørlandet.
radata: The snow data are freely available and accessed from the seNorge snow depth NetCDF files hosted through the MET Norway THREDDS service [@met_thredds]. Two datasets are included in this indicator publication under an open licence: The spatial mountain mask is read from `Fjell_norge_publisering.gdb`, layer `Modellert_fjell_50` [@blumentrath2010areal]. The regional helper file is an `sf` object containing five polygons and an `arealFjell` attribute (CC0).
arealrepresentativitet: Daily snow depth values are first temporally aggregated to a winter mean raster for each winter year. The winter mean raster is then masked to mountain areas. Spatial aggregation is carried out by calculating the arithmetic mean of all valid mountain raster cells within each of five mountain regions. The regional indicator values are aggregated to produce a national estimate.
referansetilstand: The reference condition is defined as the typical winter snow depth observed during the historical reference period 1961–1990. This period is used to represent earlier climatic snow conditions in Norwegian mountain ecosystems before the strongest recent warming signal.
referanseverdier: For each region, the x~100~ reference level is calculated as the median winter mean snow depth during 1961–1990. The median is used because snow depth can be strongly influenced by unusually snowy or unusually snow-poor winters. x~0~ is a complete abscense of snow. x~60~ is defined by observed values that are 2 sd units smaller than the snow deoths observed across the reference period. This definition of 2 sd units has been used to define extreme weather events.
annen_informasjon: The main uncertainties relate to the underlying seNorge snow depth product, the spatial delineation of mountain areas, the regional aggregation layer, and the ecological interpretation of snow depth as an indicator of condition. Mountain snow depth varies strongly over short distances due to elevation, aspect, wind exposure and local terrain. These fine-scale patterns may not be fully captured in gridded climate data. The indicator is also sensitive to the selected winter period. December-May was chosen to match the previous assessment, but other choices, such as snow-season length or date of melt-out, could represent different ecological mechanisms. Additional uncertainty arises from the selection of the 1961–1990 reference period and the assumption that historical snow conditions represent a desirable ecological reference state. Different baseline periods or alternative normalisation approaches could produce different condition scores, particularly in regions experiencing strong long-term climatic trends.
pavirkningsfaktorer: The main impact factor affecting this metric is climate change, particularly changes in winter temperature and precipitation. Natural drivers include elevation, latitude, distance from the coast, topography, wind redistribution of snow, and interannual weather variability. Land use may have local effects on snow accumulation and redistribution, but these effects are not explicitly modelled here.
version_comment: Snow depth data from seNorge has been used in other indicator version in Norway before, but this is the first version on ecRxiv.
precision: Reported as probability distributions for the true indicator value
